title: Zdravo, Sarajevo!
reviewerNotes: Exemplar chapter. ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Ana lands in Sarajevo and takes her first walk through Baščaršija, practicing greetings and new letter sounds.

vocabulary: Learn basic greetings such as zdravo, dobar dan, hvala, and molim
Walk the full Latin Bosnian alphabet, including č ć š ž đ dž lj nj
grammar: Learn all 30 Latin Bosnian letters from A to Ž, with sound examples
Type accented letters on a plain keyboard
Use simple greeting exchanges before full conjugation
culture: See Baščaršija as Sarajevo’s old bazaar heart
Use warm everyday greetings in Bosnia and Herzegovina

grammar.title: The full Latin Bosnian alphabet
grammar.explanation: Learn this as a full phrase. Do not treat it as a table. Bosnian in this course uses the Latin script only. There is no Cyrillic here. There are 30 letters. Most match English shapes, and a few need extra care. Say the full order out loud. The letters are A B C Č Ć D Dž Đ E F G H I J K L Lj M N Nj O P R S Š T U V Z Ž.

grammar.title: Writing č ć š ž đ
grammar.explanation: Treat this as a ready chunk you can say today. Bosnian uses letters that many English keyboards do not show by default. You need č ć š ž đ, and the capitals Č Ć Š Ž Đ. You must write them correctly from the start.

grammar.title: Greeting exchanges
grammar.explanation: Say the whole line together. Skip the full chart for now. Start simple. Say a greeting, hear one back, then add hvala or molim. Formal day greetings use dobar dan. Friends often say zdravo.

culture.title: Baščaršija, Sarajevo’s old heart
culture.body: Baščaršija is the historic bazaar of Sarajevo. Narrow streets, copper shops, cafés, and the sound of footsteps on stone. Ana arrives with a backpack and a phrase list. Shopkeepers greet visitors with a warm Dobar dan! Learning greetings here is not just polite. It opens doors (and often a free smile). The special letters in Baščaršija (š, č) are your first real Bosnian workout.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Walk the full alphabet
lessonBlocks.body: Say the whole Latin Bosnian alphabet out loud once. The letters are A B C Č Ć D Dž Đ E F G H I J K L Lj M N Nj O P R S Š T U V Z Ž. That is thirty letters. Digraphs Dž, Lj, and Nj are single alphabet letters even though they look like two characters. Now zoom in on the ones English does not have. Practice Č č like church, Ć ć a bit softer and shorter, Dž dž like jam, Đ đ a softer j, Š š like ship, and Ž ž like the s in measure, plus Lj lj and Nj nj. Practice the words čaj, ćup, džezva, đak, šuma, žena, ljubav for love, and njega for care. Ana drills them on the plane, then spots Baščaršija on a sign and finally hears the letters in a real street name.
tips: Do not skip the boring letters. C sounds like ts, and J sounds like English Y.
Č is harder. Ć is softer and shorter.
Write č ć š ž đ correctly. Do not replace them with plain c s z d.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. Your first greetings
lessonBlocks.body: Memorize this mini set as full words. Zdravo means hi. Dobar dan means good day. Dobro jutro means good morning. Dobra večer means good evening. Hvala means thanks. Molim means please or you are welcome. Doviđenja means goodbye. Da means yes. Ne means no. Use Dobar dan with people you do not know well. Use Zdravo with friends, or with Emir once you meet him tomorrow. Notice that doviđenja needs đ and večer needs č. Write the special letters carefully when you practice.
tips: A smile helps more than perfect pronunciation.
Learn each greeting as a ready chunk. Do not treat it as a grammar puzzle.
If you forget, Hvala still works almost everywhere.

funFacts.title: Baščaršija means main market
funFacts.body: Baščaršija is not just a pretty old-town label. The name comes from Turkish roots for the chief marketplace. Craft shops, cafés, and copper work still fill those streets today. When Ana learns greetings here, she is practicing language in a living market rather than a museum set.

funFacts.title: One letter, one sound
funFacts.body: Bosnian spelling is mostly phonetic, which helps beginners a lot. What you see is usually what you say once the special letters click. Letters like č, ć, š, ž, and đ each carry one clear sound. That predictability is why Lesson 1 spends real time on the alphabet before long conversations.

funFacts.title: Cats of the čaršija
funFacts.body: Sarajevo’s old town is famous for friendly street cats. They claim doorsteps, café chairs, and warm stone with total confidence. Mrvica is fictional, but her attitude matches that local habit. If a cat joins your language practice in Baščaršija, you are having a very Sarajevo lesson.

questions.question: What does 'zdravo' mean?
questions.explanation: Zdravo is the friendly everyday hello.

questions.question: Which greeting is more polite with strangers during the day?
questions.explanation: Dobar dan is the polite daytime greeting.

questions.question: Which word means 'thank you'?
questions.explanation: Hvala = thank you. Molim can mean please or you're welcome.

questions.question: How many letters are in the Latin Bosnian alphabet?
questions.explanation: Latin Bosnian has 30 letters. Dž, Lj, and Nj each count as one letter.

questions.question: The letter š sounds most like English…
questions.explanation: Š is like sh in ship. as in Baščaršija.

questions.question: A džezva is…
questions.explanation: Džezva is the little pot used for Bosnian coffee.

questions.question: How do you say goodbye?
questions.explanation: Doviđenja means goodbye. The letter đ Needs the letter đ.

questions.question: Baščaršija is…
questions.explanation: Baščaršija is the historic market heart of Sarajevo.

questions.question: Which pair shows a harder vs softer 'ch'-like sound?
options: dž vs đ only as vowels
questions.explanation: Č is harder. Ć is softer. a classic beginner pair.

civicContext.title: International oversight still sits above elected offices
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina still has an internationally appointed High Representative with powers that can override local politics. The Office of the High Representative was created after the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement to oversee civilian implementation of the deal. Under the Bonn Powers, that office can impose laws and remove public officials. In plain terms, final legal authority does not always rest with voters and elected institutions alone.
